utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Lisa Biersay, case manager Thomas Laugel, and legal intern Simona Gabriel Onicel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell and our legal intern Ms. Kaitlin McKenzie. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If there's nothing for the moment -- Mr. Gosnell?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the witness can be brought in while I put something on the record with Your Honour's leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. The witness may be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I apologise for the Chamber. There was a dead-line of yesterday by noon to report back to you about two video-clips that had been used with Witness GH45, and we did come to an agreement with the Prosecution on the two clips. And just for the record, the two clips that are now tendered are 1D589, which is an extract of 65 ter 5030 and that's already been marked as D86. And then 1D590 is an extract of 5033, which is already marked as D87 and the clips have been provided to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So the new clips are admitted and marked and the two old numbers will be vacated, Madam Registrar? [Trial Chamber and Registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay, the new ones will get those numbers. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Negga.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I remind you that you are still under oath. Mr. Gosnell, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Negga. How are you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could I ask the assistance of the court usher. I would, to facilitate proceedings, ask that the 92 ter statement be distributed to the court officer and the Legal Officer so we can avoid switching back and forth between the statement and the documents on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mrs. Negga, by the time you arrived in Sector East, did you know or did you hear that there were already --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I ask that the -- I believe the witness already has a -- her 92 ter statement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So I made three copies for the Judges and one for the Legal Officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Mrs. Negga. When you arrived there, did you know or did you learn that there were already tens of thousands, at least, of persons of Serbian ethnicity who had been displaced from Western Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only learnt that after I arrived in Belgrade because when I was asked to join the mission, I was destined for Sector North. And when I got to Belgrade, I was told that that decision had to be changed because my predecessor -- the persons who were previously in Sector East had elected to return to New York and that a presence was needed there urgently and I was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how many displaced persons from Western Slavonia of Serbian ethnicity were you told were in Sector East, approximately? I understand how long it's been, but in general terms, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what point are you talking?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm talking about upon your arrival.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, upon my arrival it was about a week or two before it was certain that I would be in Sector East, so at that point we were not very much concerned with numbers. It was only when I attended my first meeting with the local authorities in Vukovar and later in Beli Manastir that numbers were being pushed around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And they told you that there were already a very large number --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That had been displaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: These are not people who had been brought by the authorities. Weren't these people who had been -- who had fled there out of necessity?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were these individuals who had fled to Sector East out of - at least as they perceived it - necessity?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that there were refugees from other parts of the former Yugoslavia that were coming into Sector East. Is that what you're asking me? Because the "fleeing" I don't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me come at this from another direction. I'm right that Western Slavonia is in Croatia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in order to get to Sector East from Western Slavonia you have to pass through Bosnia; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is that the route -- would you know the route that many or most of those displaced persons used to get to Sector East? Do you know what towns they might have passed through?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that that was one of the routes, but they would suddenly disappear overnight. So one was never quite sure as to the many routes or the exact route that they took.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you hear that in some cases families were separated such that the men who had fled from Western Slavonia went to Sector East when it was -- when there was still a time of armed conflict and women and children or the elderly sometimes stayed behind in Bosnia or in Serbia before rejoining their husbands or sons or fathers?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall that we were told in the meetings that nightly busloads of women, children, and men would be brought into the Baranja and later on into Sector East -- into other parts of Sector East, but as to how they were separated and when they were separated, I couldn't tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The reason I'm asking you these questions is because of what you say at paragraph 66 in your statement. And for the record, you've also addressed this issue at paragraphs 25, 58, 70, and 108 to 112.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's -- perhaps we could just start on 66 and we'll go to some others if we need to.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You say here: "I reported on 2 July 1992 that there were 17.000 Serb refugees brought to the Baranja from Bosnia. More were expected. Throughout this period I reported that Serbs continued to arrive to the area in large numbers."

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were figures supplied by my civil affairs officer resident in Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let's take a look at one of the documents that you prepared that appears to echo this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05197, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Indeed, this is the footnote there at footnote 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this is your report to Mr. Thornberry of the 2nd of July, 1992, and there in the first full paragraph - and we can expand to the page width for the assistance of the witness - it says: "The co-ordinator of refugees into the Baranja, Ms. Constantonovic reported that so far 17.000 persons had been brought to the Baranja from Bosnia-Herzegovina and that more were expected." Is that what you were?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, I -- the reason I ask -- well, let -- and it says previous to that at the top of the page: "He added that the community was traumatised..." and this is referring, I believe, to the words of Dr. Mutanzic [phoen] who worked at the Baranja medical centre. "He added that the community was traumatised by the war and was experiencing psychological and material stress as a result of the influx of refugees from Bosnia-Herzegovina ..." Did they tell you from where precisely in Bosnia these refugees originated?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, what you see is the report that I received from the Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you're sure that you were told that these refugees originated from Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Were you told anything about what fighting had led to this departure?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did they explain to you why Serbs would be fleeing Bosnia, whereas, based on the information I have, they were able to flee to the extent they were displaced to the Autonomous Region of Krajina and to the Republika Srpska, which was within Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, my understanding is that to the extent Serbs -- people of Serbian ethnicity in Bosnia were being displaced, they were displaced to other areas of Bosnia, namely the Autonomous Region of Krajina or the Republika Srpska, and that in fact there were no people or almost no people of Serbian ethnicity fleeing from Bosnia anywhere, including the Baranja.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But the Baranja was part of Sector East, the occupied territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is it possible that you misunderstood what you were told about the origin of these people who were -- who had come or who were coming to the Baranja?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no possibility of any misunderstanding because the reports were not given verbally. They were mostly in writing. Or when I was actually in the Baranja to attend meetings. So it wasn't a hearsay situation. It was a written or a reporting that was actually documented at the time the statement was made.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, I've looked at your reports, including this report, and here we see information being conveyed about the number and the origin of these individuals. And there's no indication of the source of the information being written down or being documentary. Indeed, it seems that the source is oral. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Couldn't be. There was no means of an oral communication between the Baranja and Erdut. There were reports that were sent via the computer or they were sent by a messenger.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And who was Ms. Constantonovic?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it says, she was the co-ordinator for refugees into the Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Affiliated with what institution or body?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was she part of the UN or --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was she a local official?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I presume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So are you saying that she sent you or someone in Sector East HQ a written communication about this?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, she would have sent it to the civil affairs officer in the Baranja, who reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you can't say whether that civil affairs officer may have understood what he or she was being told about the origin of these individuals arriving?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's have a look at another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05190, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is your report of the 22nd of June, 1992, to Mr. Thornberry. If we could go to page 4. Now at the very top of the page there under "Observations," it says: "In view of the influx of Serbians into the Sector ..." Now, let's just stop there. Are you reporting here - and I don't know whether you can recall so I'll just first of all ask you whether you can recall this - are you saying that as of June 1992 there was an ongoing influx of people of Serb ethnicity into Baranja?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, yes. And not only the Baranja. They came over into areas -- into other towns and -- or villages. Because throughout the reports, you were -- you would observe where the minorities were asked to have them as guests in the house because there was no available accommodation or they were just put in houses. So there was a stream of Serbs coming into Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And down at the bottom of the page, same page that we're on: "At the same time the Serbianisation of the sector continues - especially in the Baranja where busloads of tired-looking older persons, and children are seen to enter via Batina bridge on a regular basis." Now, is that description of older persons and children, isn't that consistent with people re-joining their husbands, their fathers, their sons?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does appear to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you have any estimates at all - and I know that it's been a very long time - it's just that in your reports and in your 92 ter statement you don't give precise information about this. How many Serbs entered Sector East let's say in the second half of 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no means of counting them one by one. We just noticed that there was an obvious increase in the number and also from the complaints we received from minorities, that they were being urged to leave their houses to the newcomers or to accept them as guests, indicated that there were clearly newcomers to this sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But those complaints could just as easily have arisen, could they not, from harassment or pressure caused by the large number of displaced persons who were already there prior to your arrival?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "the large number of displaced persons who were ... there ..."?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me put my cards completely on the table to try to explain what I'm getting at.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: My position is that by June 1992 virtually the movement of displaced persons had already occurred and that after June 1992, while it's true that there were some others arriving, the numbers were quite small relative to the movements that occurred earlier. And that's what I'm getting at, and so now I'm asking you whether the complaints that you received about harassment, wouldn't they be equally consistent with pressure from displaced persons, Serbs, who arrived before June 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, in paragraph 66, and I'm focusing on this, you say that they were brought to the Baranja. Who do you say brought them?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Busloads came, so obviously they were brought, but as to who brought them I cannot tell you because I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we look at paragraph 113 of your statement, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And while that's coming up or while we're turning to that, we could also bring up 01035, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, here you refer to a law being passed allowing the confiscation of non-Serb property on mere allegations that non-Serbs collaborated with the enemy. Do you remember what the title of that law may have been?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Because the local authorities kept promising to supply us with the laws and they never did. The reports were mainly received through CIVPOL who had to investigate each case of intimidation or harassment or whatnot and give a reporting on the reasons or the conversations they held with the prosecutor or whatever the local judicial authority consisted of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could just slightly expand the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this, Madam, is a law of the Government of the RSK. It's dated apparently the 21st of April, 1992, and it's called -- well, I must correct myself. It's not a law. It's called a decision on the return of refugees. And Article 1 says that a request must be sent and then Article 2 says that a check must be carried out to verify if the individual was directly or indirectly involved with any enemy unit or nationalist and fascist party. Is it possible that this is the provision that you intended to refer to insofar as this would appear to potentially exclude individuals from returning who fell within that category?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible, but as I said we had been promised a copy of the decision and we were never given one. We merely had to quote what was told to us by the Serbian prosecutor or his workers.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now if we could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Article 5: "A person who was authorised to return to the territory of the Republic shall be allowed to have unhindered access to his/her earlier place of residence and have equal rights like all other citizens of the Republic in accordance with the Constitution and the laws of the Republic." Now, do you remember that -- seeing that provision?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember hearing or seeing about this decision at all?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that it existed, but I never saw it in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this decision makes no distinction at all based on whether or not a person previously left Sector East with or without a declaration saying that they were leaving voluntarily; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me back up and put it a different way. Yesterday you suggested that the RSK authorities sought to obtain certificates from individuals, Croats or non-Serbs, who wanted to leave Sector East, saying that they were leaving voluntarily. And as I understood what you were saying yesterday, you thought that they were doing that in order to deprive them of the right to return. Did I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes in part, and also to say that since they were leaving their property became the property of the Serbian state or the Krajinian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you say that that depended on the issuance of such a certificate, in particular if they were leaving voluntarily then there could be this forfeiture to the state that you're describing?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they leave voluntarily there would be a forfeiture, not could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But no mention of this in this decision, is there?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I told you, I haven't seen this decision in writing. I'm just telling you what happened on the ground. Once they leave, they had to declare that they were leaving voluntarily. That being done, their property was confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, was it confiscated or rather was it put at the temporary use of the local authorities?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not willing to go into semantics. If they took the property and placed people in them, the property was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's take a look please at 01469. Now, Mrs. Negga, this is a report from someone named Tomislav Papic and it's dated the 2nd of February, 1993. And he is the secretary of the secretariat for the civil engineering and urban planning in the Serb district of SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can go to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He's describing the work of a commission for the registering and allocation of houses for accommodation and flats. If we could just scroll down. Now, there at the bottom of the page it says: "The Commission works on checks relating to cases of moving in and relocation and they issue the first temporary decisions for all housing units now occupied." If we can turn the page. I won't go through this entire page with you, Mrs. Negga, chapter and verse, but if you just look at this page what you'll see is frequent reference to "temporary accommodation" and "temporarily accommodated." Do you remember anyone at all from the local authorities telling you that those displaced persons who had come to Sector East, that they were being temporarily accommodated in houses?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the use of the word "temporarily." The saying was that these people were in the sector, housing was -- and there was a shortage of housing, and they had to be either put with minorities to live or they had to be given unoccupied housing. But there was never any mention of "temporary."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did Mr. Ilic ever tell you that he expected those who had left, those of non-Serb ethnicity, did he ever tell you that he expected those individuals to return?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he said that he didn't think they would return because they had either collaborated with the enemy - meaning Croatia - or they had left voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05186, please, Prosecution tab 14. I had thought that 01469 was already an exhibit, but now I am informed that it's not, and therefore I would tender that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D90, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The number again is 5186.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, Mrs. Negga, this is a report that was sent to you on the 16th of June, 1992, by Yolanda Auger to you. It appears to include an attachment with an article from a Hungarian-language publication. If we could turn to page 2. I won't turn to it, but just for your information on the last page of this document the Hungarian original appears and it seems that the speaker is Milan Ilic. Now, down there, the bottom paragraph, the questioner seems to say: "It can hardly be said that Baranja is overflowed with tourists." And then it seems that there is an answer: "The refugees are expected to return. According to Mr. George Latas, only about 3% of the refugees could be accused of some sort of plot against the Serbian authorities. As far as the others are concerned, they should come to no harm." Did Mr. Ilic -- and I presume that Mr. Ilic would have wanted to impress upon you that he was co-operative and believed in the spirit of the Vance Plan. He never expressed this sentiment to you?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But you did receive this?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you ever ask Mr. Ilic about this information?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mrs. Negga, that the main reason why non-Serbs were leaving Sector East was intimidation, terrorisation, acts of violence against them?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: And loss of jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We'll come to that reason as well, but would you say that the primary impetus was indeed these threats or these acts of violence?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And were the majority, most of these acts of violence, did they take place under cover of darkness, at night-time?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is it right that the perpetrators would often masquerade in JNA uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I have a -- is counsel referring to a paragraph in Mrs. Negga's statement for that proposition?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, it's paragraph 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But, Mrs. Negga, even without looking at your statement, do you remember that that's the way it was?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I remember in Ilok that is the way it was. But for other parts of the sector --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, there it says -- the very next line says: "I was told that these tactics were used not only in Ilok but also in Erdut and Beli Manastir."

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So these tactics were used throughout Sector East?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: But primarily in Ilok, where the perpetrators would be able to cross the Backa Palanka and escape into Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, are you saying that people were coming in from Serbia and terrorising the local population in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me put it this way. As explained to me by Mr. Spanovic, the minister of defence, the intent was to build a corridor from Knin to Serbia to connect the Serbian residents between those two points, going up to the Baranja, hence there was a movement of people between Serbia and Sector East. Whether they lived in Sector East or they came from Serbia, I cannot tell you. But according to our CIVPOL there was a movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you agree that in the vast majority of cases of intimidation, violence, in particular violence, the victims were not able to identify specifically the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to agree to that because the victims who reported to UNPROFOR and who sought UNPROFOR help to either have these harassments stopped or to assist them to cross the confrontation line, they knew the people who were victimising them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are you saying that they named them?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many cases they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: "Many cases," but I'm asking you about the majority of cases. Wasn't it the case -- certainly there were cases where individuals were named, certainly. My question is in the majority, and I say the vast majority of cases, wasn't it the case that the victims were not able to identify by name the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your use of the word "majority of cases," you know, somewhat would put me in a corner because there were many cases where they could not identify, but I could not tell you whether they were the majority or the minority or a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Fair enough. Thank you, Mrs. Negga. Let's look at some documents that describe some of the acts of violence that were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 05190, please. If away go to page 4 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And we were just looking at this document, this is your report to Mr. Thornberry of the 22nd of June. Yes, it's page 4 at the top of the page but it's actually page 5 of e-court. It says there just below "Beli Manastir": "In the past there have been in the past week cases of torture, maltreatment of minorities and increasing activity of street gangs and irregular, including members of the milicija and special police (Red Berets) against members of minorities." Now, I see that there's an adjective used there without a noun, "irregular." Did you mean -- what did you mean there, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the term was used in the same sense as was used when reference was made to the movement of the JNA, the Serbian irregulars, and such-like on the hospital in Vukovar. That is the meaning of the term "irregular."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So there we seem to have irregulars, street gangs, and also members of the milicija and the Red Berets all participating in these acts of violence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you remember on what you based the identification of these four groups?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been on the reports of CIVPOL, the reports of the civil affairs officers in the different areas, and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And also based on information given to you by the local police?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When confronted by CIVPOL, the local police would reply that these were the responsible parties. But the local police never gave me directly any information. They interfaced with CIVPOL. That was CIVPOL's duty, to deal with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is any of this report under Beli Manastir based on any of your direct communication with local officials?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had talks with Dr. Musavic [phoen], who was head of the medical, whenever he appealed for assistance for medicines or help in curbing the refugee influx. But as I said, there was resident in Beli Manastir a civil affairs officer, so my presence was not needed directly. It was his responsibility to collect information, report to me, and then I reported to the director of civil affairs, Mr. Cedric Thornberry. That was the line of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And it says here: "Local authorities are dissociating themselves from these incidents claiming that there are individuals and groups acting on their own. Regrettably, co-operation with them is excellent in theory but not in practice." And then it says: "According to the statement of the police commander, patrolling has become impossible due to the blockade." What blockade was in effect that would have anything to do with patrolling at this time?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certain areas that the civil -- CIVPOL was not allowed to enter. The Serbs blocked them from entering certain parts of the sector and they just could not perform their work. This was all reported to Cedric Thornberry, the director of civil affairs, to have him interfere at a higher level to ensure that UNPROFOR was in no way obstructed in its duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Here we appear - and you're the author of this - it appears that it's the police commander who is complaining about this blockade. Am I wrong in thinking that this reference to "police commander" is the local police commander?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be -- it would not be the local police. It would be the CIVPOL police that are saying we're not allowed to go into certain areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The next sense then says: "At all local officials level, due to the present economic and political problems as a result of the sanctions, coping with existing problems is impossible. This is, indeed, the usual answer that UNPROFOR is getting from those authorities." Now, does that jog your memory at all that the reference to the blockade is really a reference to the sanctions that were preventing oil from reaching Sector East, petrol?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, the sanctions did work against the sector insofar as there was no oil to move around.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that affected the local police's ability to patrol; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, they claimed that it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that the local police were also -- they feared patrolling because they considered that it was too dangerous, especially at night?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear that armed UNPROFOR patrols were shot at when they patrolled at night?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You never heard that the local patrols were equally targeted?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that they patrolled at night, but there's one difference. UNPROFOR could not return fire. UNPROFOR was just there as a barrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We'll come later to UNPROFOR's functions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could turn the page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just so you know, Mrs. Negga, what I'm trying to do with this document and the succeeding documents is to take us through chronologically so we have a good sense of context. So we're going to jump sometimes from one issue to the next. Under "Ilok" it says here: "However, the head of the milicija in Babske ... (an immigrant Serb) was found to be intimidating minorities and was dismissed from his job." Now let me just stop there. Can you remember by whom he was dismissed, this immigrant Serb, head of the milicija?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would have been by the local authorities. Only they had the authority to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you understand that he was removed because he had been intimidating authorities?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Then it says: "CIVPOL report that the milicija seem genuine in their desire to uphold the Law." Do you know and can you help us understand on what basis they told you that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me they believed the militia when they said they wanted things to be quiet.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn please to 05193.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And this is your report of the 25th of June to Mr. Thornberry. If we just look at the second paragraph, we've just seen a reference, Mrs. Negga, to an immigrant Serb and then here in this second paragraph we see reference to: "An incident occurred at Ilok on ... 20 June - some 500 Serbs demonstrated against UNPROFOR ..." And then there are a series of complaints. I know that subsequently you did participate in meetings with Serb immigrants in Ilok. Am I right that this group that is demonstrating, they are the immigrants, the recently arrived immigrants to the area?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. My meetings in Ilok was mainly with the Slovak and Croatian and other minorities who were under stress.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Okay. We'll come to that. If we could turn to page 3, please -- actually, we could start, perhaps, with page 2. Here it says, referring to Mr. Ilic in that second full paragraph: "He eventually returned to the purpose of our meetings and pledged that at future meetings all local heads would be present and if we were unable to solve problems these could be specifically discussed at which point the local leaders will be called to account." Is that what Mr. Ilic told you, that he would discipline those that he could discipline for not performing their tasks properly?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right. But as I repeatedly wrote to Mr. Thornberry, we received assurances but the situation never changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's turn to page 3. You describe your meeting with Mr. Kvesic. Again we see a reference at the beginning of this paragraph to 25- to 30.000 newcomers arriving from Serbia and Bosnia. Now, was Mr. Kvesic giving you the same information that you were receiving from the Serb side about the origin of the immigrants?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, they both said from Bosnia-Herzegovina and sometimes added "other parts of the former Yugoslavia," without specifying what the other parts were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And Mr. Kvesic is reported here as that: "He commended UNPROFOR on its work in that region, in particular BELBAT's regular patrolling as well as CIVPOL's investigatory activities and civil affairs' assistance in dealing with expulsions, threats, and other human rights violations." Was BELBAT regularly patrolling in its area?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why were they doing that?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because there was need for patrol, the Romas, the gypsies on the Hungarian border were under constant threat, and other minorities were also under threat and the Belgians were most conscientious about their duties for UNPROFOR and their patrolled regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did they attempt to locate where non-Serb minorities tended to live? What I mean is, did they attempt to focus their patrolling geographically to protect non-Serb minorities?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would assume so. I can't say definitively.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you know whether -- how frequently they were patrolling?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean this is the BELBAT. You know, that was the military. I only co-ordinated the work. I didn't follow their step-by-step work.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you understand - and I think this is implied in your answers - did you understand that they were patrolling in order to restore law and order?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you understand that that was part of their mandate under the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was part of their mandate insofar as they would keep a strict eye on the local police to ensure that they carried out their functions as other international police would carry out the function in protecting and serving the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, my understanding is that the only entity that was supposed to be supervising the local police was CIVPOL, whereas UNPROFOR had a different function which didn't involve supervising the local police. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, but when there is a shortage of CIVPOL and the need arises, the UN has to work hand in hand, whether it be with the UNPROFOR, the UNHCR, or any other UN agency, we have to support each other to carry out the mandate of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Certainly. And UNPROFOR, unlike CIVPOL, is fully armed; right?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but as I said, we -- the UN military was not allowed to fire arms, it just carried arms, but it could not use force.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we go back to page 1, please. It's describing tension increasing in the area, but I'm interested in the part where it says that there were leaders of industry accusing UNPROFOR of discriminating against them and not protecting them from the dire effects of the sanctions. They claim that as a result of shortage of raw materials in Beli Manastir area, factories will be closed and approximately 400 workers will be laid off. Was the situation that severe in terms of the sanctions, that industry was forced to cease operations?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sanctions did hurt, but it was always used as an excuse by the Serbs to get rid of minorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever -- and you have reported in your statement the number of non-Serbs who were dismissed. Did you ever conduct any review as to how many Serbs lost their jobs?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we received complaints of non-Serbs losing their jobs, it was usually accompanied by the accusation that they were replaced by Serbs. So clearly there was no need to conduct an investigation as to how many Serbs lost jobs if they were being employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So if I understand correctly, to the extent that you allege that companies were discriminatorily laying off non-Serbs, it's based on the information given to you by those who were laid off or fired?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and confirmed later by my confronting the factory owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Which factory owner or owners?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, in Ilok where certain Slovaks were laid off, they would reply that it's because of the straightened economic circumstances occasioned by the sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Straightened economic circumstances, so it wasn't that they were replacing these non-Serb workers with Serb workers?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm telling you what they told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. That is what I wanted to know, thank you. So they told you that the reason for these layoffs was the straightened economic circumstances?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you observed that, in fact, there were in fact straightened economic circumstances during these times because of the sanctions; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were. The sanctions hurt the local people across the board.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And there were substantial layoffs?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the information we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So I come back to my previous question, and I know, Mrs. Negga, that it may appear redundant, and I'm so sorry for asking you what may appear to be a redundant question. It's correct you weren't able to do a statistical review of how many Serbs were laid off during this period?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have 05197, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is your telefax from the 2nd of July to Mr. Thornberry. If we could turn to page 5. "On 29 June 1992 representatives of UNPROFOR, UNHCR, and ICRC met with Serbian immigrant residents of Ilok to hear their complaints, which had been raised at a demonstration of some 500 residents on 21 June and to inform them of our frustrations and problems with their treatment of minorities ... the vocal immigrants were most radical." Does -- do you remember this meeting?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I remember this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And if we can just scroll down, there's a paragraph that begins: "The concerns expressed ..." And amongst the concerns expressed, it appears that this -- some of the individuals there expressed their determination to prevent return of minorities at all cost. Now, am I right in understanding that essentially this was a group of Serbs who were radical, extremist, and who didn't want a return of any non-Serbs to the area?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Was this fuelled by the fact that they themselves had been displaced from somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember that they were -- by their demeanour, they were radical, they were extreme, they were intransigent, I presume, to your words and the words of the other members of the delegation that met with them?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. But at every meeting the Serbs and -- didn't limit themselves to what was happening or what had happened after 1991 November. They went back into history, you know, World War II, 1792, so one -- you know, this -- it was a fusing of complaints and anger and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, it's one thing to talk about historical matters and to know one's history --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- and to know the origins of a conflict, but it's another to express the views that are set out in this paragraph. And the question that I have for you is: Did you observe that there was a distinction between recently arrived immigrants - and I understand this is a generalisation - there was a distinction between the views of recently arrived immigrants and those who were long-time residents of the area?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't answer that because I couldn't distinguish as to who was who. You know, I didn't know the long-standing -- the long-term -- long-standing residents and the recent ones, but some were more vocal than others.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, we have seen two documents where you've managed to draw the distinction between local residents and newly arrived immigrants because we have the police commander in Bapska being removed who is identified as a Serb immigrant, and then we have this group that is identified as a group of immigrants. So apparently you were able to draw some distinction on occasion?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: On occasion, on occasion we were.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 7, please. Actually, let's start with page 8 and we'll go back to page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Under "miscellaneous," the last line: "In many areas the immigrant Serbs are the main troublemakers and retaliators." Do you remember that that was your impression?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because that was reported to me by CIVPOL who had their information from the local police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let's turn to the previous page. "Mr. Stojanovic, the Mayor of the village who is influential as well as his wife ... who deals with refugees, has promised to assist in calming down the tension in the village. They recognised the existence of extremists who get drunk and terrorise the people during the night. The Mayor stated that the Blue Brigades (special police or milicija) are involved in cases of harassment. Their commanders are requested to reorganise them and remove those who misbehave. He also mentioned that all local officials in the Baranja had received clear instructions from high officials of the Krajina to that effect." Now, do you remember that instructions, whether from any source, whether it's this information or any other source, that indeed such instructions were being issued --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- by, as it says, here "high officials of the Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: We merely reported what we were told.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's what you're doing here?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 5200, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is the 6th of July, so it's four days after the previous document. Now, I just want to start with that second paragraph which takes us into a slightly different topic. This is describing the voluntary certificate that is required to be obtained. And it says here that Mr. Ilic and all local authorities are adamant on this requirement. Did you ever hear or did it occur to you that, in fact, Mr. Ilic and the others had instituted the requirement of this certificate because they didn't want people leaving Sector East willy-nilly? By "people," I mean non-Serbs.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't occur to me because on occasion the council would ask us to help non-Serbs to cross the confrontation line.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Certainly there were occasions - and I understand the criteria that may have been applied by you and by them to determine that - but what I'm getting at is: Why would there be -- why would they reserve the right to delay departure, if you know, by up to 90 days to consider the matter?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could it be because they, just as you, were concerned that they didn't want accusations coming from you, or from the Croats for that matter, that they were colluding, facilitating the departures of these individuals without adequate cause?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was put to us that this was the policy to be adhered to. What their reasons, I don't know, but if it's their policy - and they told us it was their policy - that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So they never at all told you what the reasons for the policy were?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Each time it was that the reason had been made above or they had to seek permission to give us information as to what was happening or to change any -- any practice, and that was it. They couldn't exercise much initiative on the ground. They said they would have to get permission from above or from Knin to do certain things or to answer certain questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn, please, to 5202.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is your note to Mr. Thornberry dated the 9th of July. If we turn over to page 2, this is where you describe the incident of you being stopped at a check-point. It says at the bottom of that first paragraph: "The milicija man arrived, identified himself, and apologised for the inconvenience after some ten minutes and requested us to leave. He was clearly nervous, as one bandit walked around agitatedly ..." I just wanted to ask you about that. Why did you describe the one individual as a bandit?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that was the description given to any civilian who took arms and took the law into his hands. He was described as a bandit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And as far as you were concerned, that was what that person at the check-point was?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a civilian with arms, threatening.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And the milicija man was fearful of this individual?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, he was nervous.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 5207, please. I'm terribly sorry, can we stay on the current document for one more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we go to page 4, the last two sentences concern people being settled temporarily in houses and it's talking about settling refugees in houses. It says: "... while the number of refugees arriving to Ilok exceeded 30.000. It is understood that the commission was created on the local level and their action have no legal authority; they can move people from one house to another only according to their own judgement. Thus, they can move by force a family of two, occupying a big house, to a smaller one. To the question whether this policy applies only to the houses occupied by non-Serbs, he answered that Serbs too are being resettled now. The earlier information provided by UNPROFOR CIVPOL confirms this fact, since they have been receiving complaints from Serbs on the subject." Do you remember that the lack of accommodation in Ilok was so severe that, indeed, both Serbs and non-Serbs were being shuffled around in order to accommodate refugees?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the information provided by CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did that situation get worse as it was getting progressively colder throughout 1992?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 5207, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is from you to Yolanda Auger, referring to some individuals who were expelled on the 4th and the 10th of July. And assistance was provided by UNPROFOR for their departure. And it says here: "On both occasions both" -- perhaps we could enlarge. "On both occasions both UNPROFOR ... commander and CIVAFF (Abdul Aziz and Felesinger) tried to persuade the individuals to reconsider their decision to leave the Baranja. In the case of those listed on the 10 July from Darda, BELBAT soldiers were posted in the houses of 2 families for two nights to ensure their safety. When the local police (milicija) protested that there were unable to guarantee the safety of those individuals, arrangements were made for their crossing into Osijek." Now, my first question is, why didn't -- if you know, you may not know, but why didn't BELBAT stay there permanently at these houses to protect these individuals?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The BELBAT Battalion had a large area to patrol and its function was not to stay there permanently. They were just to secure immediate safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So they didn't have the resources?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn to page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this concerns a meeting, on page 3, and this is your report of the 17th of July to Mr. Thornberry. This concerns your meeting with a prosecutor, a local prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I may have called the wrong number. Could I have 5209.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: At page 3 the heading says "meetings." So does that mean -- when it says "meetings" in your documents, does that mean that you attended the meeting that's reported?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In many instances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So it describes your meeting with Mr. Milorad Trosic, along with Larry Moore, and Mr. Trosic is describing to you his activities, and it's describing the Tovarnik case. "He further volunteered that the case had been upgraded from the original charges at the initiative of the Court System. He explained the stages of a case, which necessitates a second, thorough investigation by the Public Prosecutor's office, on the directive of the Judge. He further stated that the criminal code had been developed in co-ordination with UNPROFOR." Let's stop there. Is that right, that the criminal code was developed in conjunction or in consultation with --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: He goes on or you go on in your report: "The Tovarnik docket was presented to the Judge who has remanded it to the Prosecutor for further, thorough investigation. Much discussion was held during this reporting. CAC expressed dismay at the slow pace at which the investigation was conducted and remarked on the axiom that 'justice delayed is justice denied.' CIVPOL also expressed surprise that a request would be presented to UNPROFOR to return persons to an area where they had been and would be in physical danger. Mr. Trosic endorsed that he would request from UNPROFOR the return of the 22 expellees to receive their statements. We await the request. The accused were in the UNPA, their passports had been withdrawn, and they were under limited custody. CAC has information to the contrary." Now, do you remember, is that -- was that the nature of the conversation, the prosecutor was saying: I need to take statements from the individuals who are victims and the civil affairs commission -- not you, it's -- the CIVPOL reaction is: Well, how on earth do you expect these people to come back and give statements under current conditions. Is that the essence of it?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Is that a problem that would have applied to other cases of expulsion?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they were required to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you ever hear judges, investigating judges, express the view that they were required as a matter of procedure to take those statements from those individuals in person?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, let me just repeat -- sorry, I don't want to cut you off.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you yourself hear or did you ever hear from anyone else who was reporting to you other occasions when judges expressed the view that they needed to take statements from witnesses in person?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I see the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gosnell. Mrs. Negga, this is the time for our first break, 30 minutes. We will be back at 11.00. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm told that I have approximately ten minutes left of my allotted time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I would request a little bit more time. I think I can complete in 30 minutes, approximately. If Your Honours wish, I can motivate the request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let me -- I think that won't be a problem, Mr. Gosnell. Your re-direct, Ms. Biersay, will not be extremely long? I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Not extremely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Not so that we will get into trouble today?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: No, I don't see us certainly going beyond 1.00 and I will endeavour to make it very focused. Of course, it depends on what's raised in the next 30 minutes. And I do plan on playing a video and that may have some logistic issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we will finish before 2.00?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think that's safe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Or even at or we're here until 2.00. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Could we turn to the next page of the document that we already have.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And just to remind you, Mrs. Negga, this is your 17th of July, 1992, report to Mr. Thornberry. And this again is Mr. Trosic speaking apparently to you. It says: "He explained that the local authorities were aware of the unprofessional behaviour of some milicija and had established a Police Training School at Knin to correct the situation. He emphasised that only temporary custody of houses (e.g. in Vukovar was given to newcomers and that the new laws recognised private ownership ..." Now, I asked you a question about this earlier and you said you never remembered local officials mentioning that these accommodation arrangements were temporary. Does that jog your memory that --

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then I stand corrected because if it's in my report that he did say that, then he did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: The third paragraph down here describes a meeting with General Biorcevic, Novakovic, Jovanovic of the JNA, and chief of the investigation of the local police. UNPROFOR was represented by Colonel Malherb, Colonel Jokin, CIVPOL, and CvAO. And it says there that: "General Biorcevic and others appealed strongly to BELBAT not to implement the ultimatum in order to give more time for consultations." I presume that the ultimatum being referred to there is the need for immediate disarmament of all groups of those possessed with long-armed -- long-barrelled weapons; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume so, but as you said the CvO was there. I was not present at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What was the JNA's role at this stage, July 1992, in events in Sector East?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, there was no JNA role, but I know that our military met regularly with officers of Serbia in Belgrade that were presumably the head of JNA. But otherwise, I did not know of any official JNA presence in the sector, in the UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did it have anything to do perhaps with what you were telling us earlier about certain groups entering Sector East from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Let me be more specific. You were describing about groups entering from Serbia and engaging in intimidation and terrorisation of the local population, and in your statement you've mentioned that there was at least one incident where the JNA was present on the Backa Palanka bridge, blocking access to certain individuals. Do you know whether the JNA's role in Sector East had to do with to whom they were granting access to the area?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my reports, I recounted that the JNA were on the Serbian side of the bridge. UNPROFOR was on the bridge and the protected area side. Whenever there were incidents in Ilok and it was reported that uniforms of the JNA were being used, the sector commander, General Peters, on one or two occasions took me to Belgrade to one of his meetings with General I think it was Kosic or something to ask him to help us to curb this movement, whether it was by JNA or local people who were misusing JNA uniforms. But that was all that I knew of any contact between me and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn to 05260, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: Excuse me, may I have a tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I think it's tab 123, Prosecution tab 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, this is your letter to Mr. Ilic and attached -- and perhaps we should go to the attachment first to see what it is you were responding to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So if we could go to page 2 -- page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It says -- Mr. Ilic is writing to you on the 23rd of September. He says that: "I sent a letter immediately to our Internal Affairs Office in Vukovar, asking them to issue a permission that those people in Question can leave this territory, and go to the other (Croatian) side. "However, they informed me that a certain procedure has to be obeyed and that each person in question has to submit an application in writing, to the Internal Affairs Office in Vukovar, asking for permission to leave this territory, pointing out in this application that they want to leave this territory of their own free will." But it says that they will do it "this very day." Now if we can turn to your response at page 1, and this is in relation, Mrs. Negga, to the question I asked you earlier as to whether any of the local authorities explained why there was this policy. And if we look down at the fifth paragraph, what you say is: "Although I can understand that in normal situations one must file an application with the Internal Affairs Office in Vukovar for permission to leave the territory in order to ensure safe return in future ..." Now, it seems to me that you are expressing there what you understand to be the reason or the policy behind the rule. Do you remember where you received that information about what was the reason for the rule in normal situations?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Do you remember receiving requests from local officials for assistance in respect of law enforcement. When I say "you," I don't mean you personally. I mean in general did UNPROFOR receive requests for assistance?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would have been directed to -- if it's from the police, it would have been to CIVPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, did they ever ask UNPROFOR for assistance to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, if you're asking did they ask the civil affairs co-ordinator, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, what I'm asking is whether it was ever reported to you by anyone on the UN side that such requests had been made to UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we have 5257, please. If we could turn to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: This is your letter to Mr. Thornberry dated the 25th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on paragraph 5. "On 16 September ... Colonel Jokin, Cmdt, Maldeghem and inspector Hogue ... attended a meeting with Mr. Petrovic, President of the local community of Branjin Vrh... to discuss the increased terrorism in the village ... during the meeting, Colonel Jokin inquired if the presence of refugees from Western Slavonia and Bosnia-Herzegovina has, in a way, affected the situation in the area. Mr. Petrovic stated that some of these refugees are responsible for other crimes committed in the village since they want to seek for revenge. Colonel Jokin emphasised that terrorism in the area has greatly increased in the past weeks and that it should not be tolerated. It was finally agreed that a more established co-operation between UNPROFOR and the local authorities of Branjin Vrh be implemented to prevent further crimes in the future." Now, my question is does this in any way remind you that -- and I understand about co-ordination between CIVPOL and the police. But were there ever requests for assistance from UNPROFOR, for example, in relation to this town, Branjin Vrh, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm only reading what is here because as we said earlier BELBAT in Beli Manastir in the Baranja was quite active in protecting the non-Serbs in the area. And they would have had greater co-operation with the police there, and whatever you read is what was reported to me by BELBAT or the CvAO in the Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And given what you've just told us, that BELBAT's function at this time in Beli Manastir was to attempt to protect non-Serbs, it's probable, isn't it, based on everything you know that they would have had to co-ordinate with the local police in that function; right?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if they were undertaking work that should be done by CIVPOL, they would have to co-ordinate with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn, please, to L2.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, I can ask you, Mrs. Negga, it's right, isn't it, that the Vance Plan accorded no de jure status to the RSK?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. It was never recognised. In all the reports you would see us refer to the RSK as the "so-called republic," and this directive came directly from the Security Council. And yesterday you had asked whether at my pay grade I would have spoken to Mr. Hadzic. Since I was the co-ordinator for Sector East, it was unlikely; but if I had been appointed to Sector South, as many of my other colleagues were, they would have had contact with Mr. Hadzic because according to the UNPROFOR mandate he was the leader of the local authority and it wasn't a matter of pay grade. It was a matter of approaching authority, authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Which local authority was he the head of according to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "the Krajina"?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the so-called Krajina. It is stated to us repeatedly by the Serbs that they had established an area from Knin to the Danube on the border of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So you're saying that this authority encompassed Sector East?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm not exactly sure what difference it makes whether you were in Sector South or Sector East that a person of your pay grade would have met Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not have written directly to him on what occurred in Sector East because there was at Vukovar a council and there were in other sectors, Sector West, Sector North, there were other areas where there were established officials of the so-called Serbian Krajina. So in that particular area where we were commissioned and appointed to act, we would approach the people in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn, please, to page 9 of e-court of this document. I believe that page 9 in e-court should be page 16 up at the top. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, it says here under "basic concept": "The role of the United Nations troops would be ensure that the areas remained demilitarised and that all persons residing in them were protected from fear of armed attack. The role of the United Nations police monitors would be to ensure that the local police forces carried out their duties without discriminating against persons of any nationality or abusing anyone's human rights ..." Now, would you agree with me that what is recognised de jure here is local police forces?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And they have duties and a function under the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as all other police over the world, they were to protect the residents of their communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And not just as any other police force around the world, but this is foreseen as their function in the Vance Plan; correct?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we turn to the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Paragraph 10: "The deployment and functions of the United Nations force. "The function of protecting the inhabitants of the UNPAs would be shared between the United Nations Force's infantry units and its civilian police monitors. The infantry would ensure that the UNPAs remained demilitarised. The police monitors would ensure that the local police carried out their duties without discrimination against any nationality and with full respect for the human rights of all residents of the UNPAs." And my question is this, and we know from elsewhere in this document and from other information we have that local police were only allowed to carry sidearms. If you have a situation where you have a significantly armed group, let's call them bandits, who are committing crimes and they're heavily armed, who under the Vance Plan, according to you, has the ultimate authority to stop that -- not only authority, responsibility, if the police can't do it?

utterances.speaker: BLANDINA FRANCIS NEGGA [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a bit of a problem for the CIVPOL and the police force because if you couldn't use force, how were you going to stop them? And that was particularly brought to light with the incidents on the Batina bridge, when the Serbs sought to displace the BELBAT military and build customs offices on the Batina bridge. The United Nations was quite concerned that a war might have erupted between the Serbs and UNPROFOR, and they did everything possible to avoid that.
